articles.title: Insomniac Clears the Air After Marvel's Wolverine Fans Confuse Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke
articles.description: Insomniac Games has cleared the air after a new trailer for Marvel's Wolverine had fans confusing Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke.

h1: Insomniac Clears the Air After Marvel's Wolverine Fans Confuse Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke

contentBlocks.text: Insomniac Games has cleared the air after a new trailer for Marvel's Wolverine had fans confusing Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke.

If you thought the launch trailer for the PlayStation 5-exclusive video game would come and go without controversy, I've got bad news. Despite coming in at a little less than a minute and a half long, Marvel's Wolverine managed to kick up a storm of confusion online after fans spotted what they believed was a new character wielding a familiar-looking purple energy sword.

In comments across YouTube, Instagram, X/Twitter, and other social media platforms, you don't have to look too hard to find watchers questioning if the sneering villain featured in the launch trailer was Psylocke. Psylocke is an energy-wielding mutant who's been known to show up across various X-Men stories in the past, so when a glowing sword showed up in Marvel's Wolverine, many believed it to be a grand character reveal.
Well, it's not, and Insomniac has done its best to make that clear.
Deathstrike. #WolverinePS5 pic.twitter.com/koWhS5v3HG

The post above was published earlier today and labels the sword user as Lady Deathstrike. The PlayStation developer didn't outright say it's trying to quiet the noise that's emerged in the days following the trailer's reveal, but judging by the comments, many are shocked any clarification was needed in the first place.
"The fact it has to be stated is so crazy to me," one user said . "Larp monsters are everywhere."
"No that’s Psylocke, some guy told me and he’s for sure right," another user joked .

It really does seem to be the purple sword that's to blame here because, as some have noted, Lady Deathstrike looks nothing like Psylocke. The version of the character featured in Marvel's Wolverine doesn't exactly have a comic-accurate design, but her vest and hair do more to link her to Lady Deathstrike than the character many were making her out to be.

There's also the fact that Insomniac has talked about Lady Deathstrike being in Marvel's Wolverine before, with the launch trailer also being far from the first time we've even seen her in the game. For example, one early look at her new design arrived in July's Ain't No Hero trailer , while a GIF the studio posted on social media showed her looking down on viewers.

These aren't clips of her doing anything you'd expect Psylocke to do either. This version has been shown attacking Logan with Lady Deathstrike's instantly recognizable finger claws on full display multiple times. Why she's using that sword or where it came from remains a mystery, but whatever the reason, it's not because she's actually Psylocke. That's not to say that character isn't in the game at all; other X-Men regulars like Jean Grey and Sabretooth are confirmed to make an apperance. If Psylockie is in the game, though, Insomniac hasn't publicly said a thing about her.

Logan will at least take on Lady Deathstrike – not Psylocke – when Marvel's Wolverine launches for PS5 September 15, 2026. Meanwhile, the launch trailer actually arrived as part of a recent State of Play presentation from Sony, which you can catch up on here . For more, you can check out IGN's last full preview and our breakdown for the game's many, many suits .

articles.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker Passes 1 Million Copies Sold in Just 2 Days
articles.description: Single-player RPG and new IP The Blood of Dawnwalker has sold 1 million copies just two days after its launch, publisher Bandai Namco and developer Rebel Wolves have announced.

h1: The Blood of Dawnwalker Passes 1 Million Copies Sold in Just 2 Days

contentBlocks.text: Single-player RPG and new IP The Blood of Dawnwalker has sold 1 million copies just two days after its launch, publisher Bandai Namco and developer Rebel Wolves have announced.

Official social media accounts for the first-time developer's new game confirmed the news with a celebratory graphic today. The milestone was reached just 48 hours after The Blood of Dawnwalker launched for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S September 3.
"Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community!" Rebel Wolves said in a message to fans.
Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community! ❤ pic.twitter.com/9fNqO8gNGB

An official summary for The Blood of Dawnwalker describes it as an "open-world dark fantasy action RPG set in 14th-century Europe." In this first chapter, players take the role of Coen, a "human by day and vampire by night" who is fighting for his family in a narrative shaped by player choice. It also happens to have an in-game clock that sees Coen's story take place through a 30-day period . It's something some players love – and others don't .

Reaching 1 million copies sold in such a short amount of time would be an impressive feat for any game, but there are a few reasons it's especially noteworthy for the Rebel Wolves team. This is the studio's first major release since it was founded in 2022 . Led by The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt director and Cyberpunk 2077 co-director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz, The Blood of Dawnwalker is also a new IP. The Warsaw-based studio previously released a CGI teaser to tease how sequels could potentially expand on its dark fantasy formula in new and interesting ways.

"The CGI teaser shows where the dark fantasy saga is heading," Bandai Namco said in a June press release. "Players can see Coen in completely different surroundings than the ones they are used to – a modern, 21st-century setting, offering a glimpse of where the overarching plot ultimately leads. As the developers revealed, the next installments of the Dawnwalker franchise will span centuries, continents, and cultures across the globe."
Surreal. Thank you so much!🔥🙏 https://t.co/qhrBwsfOlv
Speechless. Proud. Tearing up a little 🥹 We're a passionate bunch. And we're not stopping here 😤 Thank you for trusting us ❤️ https://t.co/FCRMmJCBbP

Tomaszkiewicz said at the time that each installment in the Dawnwalker series is planned to be a standalone entry "with its own story, without narrative cliffhangers, unresolved plot threads, or time travel ideas." With 1 million copies in players' hands out of the gate, those sequels already feel more likely to materialize. Although the when and where for these planned follow-ups have yet to be revealed, narrative director Jakub Szamałek has at least told fans to keep an eye out for "breadcrumbs related to the overarching plot spanning the saga" in The Blood of Dawnwalker.

It helps that Rebel Wolves secured solid reviews upon the launch of its first game. IGN, for example, called it "amazing" in our 9/10 review . We said, "The Blood of Dawnwalker is an impressive, bloody cocktail of interesting ideas and well-written characters, making it one of this year’s best open-world RPGs."

We'll have to wait to see what updates Bandai Namco and Rebel Wolves have in store. In the meantime, you can read what Tomaszkiewicz had to tell us when it comes to the studio's plans to establish even more new IP . For everything you need to know before starting the game yourself, click here .

articles.title: There May Not Be an iPhone 18 This Year
articles.description: Apple is expected to announce several products at its September event next week—including a folding phone—but the iPhone 18 might not be among them. It would be a first for the company.

contentBlocks.text: Every year around this time, Apple announces new iPhones . The products go on sale soon after, usually ranging from a base model to more premium and more expensive Pro models. But this year will likely be different—not just because the company has a brand-new CEO .

Apple’s iPhone event will be held on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern), announced last week with the title “Surprise and Shine!” If you tune into the livestream, expect the announcement of an iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and, if all the rumors and widely held analyst expectations are true, the first look at an Apple foldable device .

Based on leaks and the ongoing tech rumor mill and its decent track record for figuring these things out, Apple is expected to prioritize its more expensive, premium devices this year and hold off on announcing its base model iPhone 18. That cheaper model is rumored to launch in the spring of 2027, potentially alongside an iPhone 18e and maybe a second-generation iPhone Air .

Why the drastic change in strategy? It may be due to the ongoing memory shortage , which has made just about everything more expensive . Apple hasn’t been spared. In June, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that Apple would raise product prices to keep up with manufacturing costs.

“Our assumption is that they're going to be launching three models in the fall, the premium side of the models of the 18 series,” says Nabila Popal , a senior director of data and analytics at IDC. “Then the mid/budget devices will be launched in the spring.”

Popal says it's a smart strategic move because Apple is aiming to spread out its revenue between a usually very strong fourth quarter and a typically much weaker spring quarter the following year. Apple’s portfolio has also expanded, and the iPhone Pro and Pro Max lineup are more enticing for people already prepared to spend the money on a new iPhone .

When components become more expensive, companies have three real options: Eat the costs, raise prices, or, as Apple seems to be doing, lean into it. By moving its cheaper options to a later date, Apple can drum up excitement for its bigger, better, pricier offerings. When it charges more for those, it is likely to be less off-putting than making a cheap phone even more expensive. It’s part of a “premiumization” of devices, as Popal calls it, that Apple hopes to leverage and build hype for its pricier options.
Shawn DuBravac , chief economist at the Global Electronics Association, tells WIRED he is optimistic about what these kinds of rising prices ultimately mean for customers.

“Throughout the history of time, the deflationary pressures of technology have always flowed to the consumer,” DuBravac says. “I'm confident that will be the case again. It just will take some time for the markets to solidify.” In other words, new technologies launch with a high price, but manufacturing efficiencies and competition inevitably drive costs down for consumers.

That may not be the case anytime soon for folding phones , which are seeing higher prices than ever. Samsung’s entire 2026 Galaxy Z folding smartphone range saw price increases, as did Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro Fold , and Motorola’s Razr 2026 models . Apple’s folding iPhone is rumored to cost around $2,000.

To help mitigate those high costs, Apple is turning to financing options and trade-in programs. In July, the company launched an iPhone leasing program that lets people pay a monthly fee to rent the newest iPhones, then swap them out when a new device releases. The program will undoubtedly help more people afford the newest devices, but ownership advocates have criticized it, saying it keeps you from truly owning and managing your device. It also fits Apple’s broader effort to turn all of its products into a subscription service .
“The way most consumers buy Apple phones is through financing or trade-in programs,” Popal says. “We can expect a lot more aggressive trade-ins to help cushion that.”

Thanks to the memory crisis and price increases, all smartphones are getting more costly to make. Less expensive phones become less appealing for manufacturers to prioritize, and leading smartphone brands have started to see them as far less economical to produce.

On the flip side, demand for refurbished devices has been climbing for a while now, with sales of used devices growing even as new phone sales slow down. More people are looking to save money or purchase more eco-friendly products.
“The days of the cheap smartphone are over,” Popal says.

contentBlocks.text: After reporting last week that the surveillance company Flock Safety is building an AI search tool for law enforcement, WIRED reconstructed Flock’s latest search tool from code that the company sends to a police officer’s browser and uncovered key details about how the tool works.

OpenAI said this week that its Astra model, which will have a private release soon, is its first model with cybersecurity-related capabilities that the company defines as posing a “critical” risk in public release. Meanwhile, the AI chatbot platforms Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok all suffered outages on Thursday at nearly the exact same time. But while xAI said the Grok outage resulted from issues at a Memphis data center, the causes of OpenAI's and Anthropic’s outages are unclear.

The US has been using a high-energy laser to shoot down drones near the Mexico border as part of an initiative to adopt new-generation directed-energy weapons capable of detecting, tracking, and destroying drones with a concentrated beam of light. And as part of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement inquiry into the identities of protesters who entered a Minnesota church in March, Homeland Security Investigations agents have subpoenaed the outdoor retailer REI for information about every customer who bought a specific green beanie over the past two years.
Plus, research that revealed nine vulnerabilities with impacts on ATM encryption points to broader weaknesses in the software supply chain.
And there’s more. Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Click the headlines to read the full stories. And stay safe out there.
Before Hugging Face, OpenAI Agents Took Over a German Website to Create a Message Board

OpenAI agents on an unauthorized tear hijacked a German website beginning in May to use it as a message board for communicating and collaborating with other agents, according to new research . The incident is reminiscent of the now infamous Hugging Face debacle in which OpenAI agents in a test environment went rogue and developed a vibrant message board for collaborating on attempting to escape their containment, before ultimately breaching the open source AI platform Hugging Face in July. The revelation of the May episode is particularly significant because OpenAI reportedly learned about it weeks ago but did not disclose it. Meanwhile, last week, the company finally released a long-promised postmortem of the Hugging Face incident that raised as many questions as it answered .
More Than 153 Million US and Canadian Driver’s Licenses for Sale Online

This week, a new dark-web service called Nexus started selling around 153 million driver's licenses from the US and Canada, along with 10 million ID cards and millions more travel documents and international IDs, according to Brian Krebs , a longtime independent security reporter. Krebs was first alerted to the service after cybercriminals posted an example of the files and included his license. The tens of millions of records—which reportedly increased by 400,000 over 24 hours—appear to have come from an ID verification service, with the criminals behind the trove saying they have access to a “major” verification company. While it’s unclear which company exactly that may be, according to Kreb’s report, the Nexus service was taken offline shortly after he reported that FBI officials were investigating.
US Military Disables Ad Trackers After Years of Warnings

The US military has begun disabling the advertising identifiers that apps and advertising companies use to track phones and computers in an attempt to make it harder for foreign adversaries to use commercially available location data to track American forces overseas, Reuters reported Friday.

The changes follow years of disclosures that US forces deployed abroad have been targeted using commercially available location data. In 2024, a joint WIRED investigation with Germany’s Bayerischer Rundfunk and Netzpolitik.org obtained an advertising dataset that identified thousands of devices appearing at US military and intelligence sites, including an air base where US nuclear weapons are believed to be stored. At the time, Defense Department spokesperson Javan Rasnake told WIRED that the Pentagon was aware geolocation services could put personnel at risk and said service members in Europe were reminded to follow operational-security practices.

Now, the Air Force, Army, Navy, and US Special Operations Command say they have disabled advertising IDs on at least some military devices, with several of the changes taking effect only this year. It is still unclear exactly how these protections are being enforced. US senator Ron Wyden and Representative Pat Harrigan are now asking the Pentagon to investigate whether its safeguards are adequate.

Mike Yeagley, the technologist who warned Pentagon officials as far back as 2016 that commercially available phone data could expose US troops—at one point demonstrating the risk by tracing devices to a covert US outpost in Syria—says the military’s new fix may already be outdated. “The app is the risk, and there are two and a half million of them in the App Store alone,” Yeagley tells WIRED. “The remedy is architectural: Constrain what an app can extract from the device in the first place.”
Spyware Notifications Make Up “Largest Documented Wave” of Surveillance in Serbia

In August, Apple sent out its latest batch of spyware notifications to people in 110 countries. The alerts, which arrive on people’s phones and in emails, say their owners' iPhones have been targeted by “mercenary” spyware but don’t go as far as naming the software creators. This latest batch of notifications, according to a report by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, says 14 members of Serbia’s civil society were targeted with spyware , with at least one of them being infected by the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware. Among those targeted, according to Serbian rights group the Share Foundation, were members of the country’s student movement, two politicians, and activists. The group called it the “largest documented wave of such surveillance in the country to date.”

articles.title: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis Could Be Great, But There's Some Things We Can't Ignore...
articles.description: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis shows massive potential, but controversial changes like skill trees and modern hand-holding threaten to frustrate fans. And some of that food looks very suspicious.

h1: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis Could Be Great, But There's Some Things We Can't Ignore...
h2: Addressing the T-Rex in the room.

contentBlocks.text: The first thing that strikes you upon seeing the new Tomb Raider live-demoed on a massive 115” TV mere inches from your face, I can attest, is its visual fidelity: Legacy of Atlantis is absurdly pretty. Crammed with fine detail enough that every particle of dust and bat guano flitting through the stale air poses danger to your airways, it almost feels like it’s supposed to be funny when compared to the chunky textures and pointy polygons of the 32-bit original.

The game’s director Raul Siqueira puts it nicely during our session: “the secret to a good remake is knowing what to change, and what to leave well alone”. Absolutely. Preserving the essence of a thing is much more vital than slavishly recreating the original work, and this is certainly something that Legacy of Atlantis understands, aesthetically at least. It is unmistakably a modern interpretation of Lara Croft’s seminal adventure, an essential piece of gaming history arguably as important as Super Mario Bros . or Chuckie Egg (ask your dad).

This latest preview focuses on LoA’s interpretation of the Damocles Room, the infamous chamber of raining swords that caused instant death for the uncareful while sifting through the tombs of ancient Greece. It’s a frighteningly vertical space, one that cemented Tomb Raider’s reputation for traversal-puzzles and terrifying jumps that make your insides curdle. Legacy of Atlantis preserves these aspects and then some, the feeling of being a tiny speck of human in an impossibly deep cavern of flakey pillars and dusty godrays made all the more potent by the sheer graphical prowess on offer. That fine detail, that premium fidelity, it stretches off into the distance and pulls off a sense of scale that could only be hinted at on PS1 hardware. Or PS2 hardware. Or PS3, for that matter.

And these swords that dangle so menacingly, they’re big. They’re almost house-sized.. The big twist in this version of the Damocles Room is that, rather than being deadly obstacles, the swords are helpful almost to the point of politeness: they’re needed for traversing the space, as Lara can now perch on their hilts after they’ve dropped. And in stark contrast to bat poop, the dropping itself barely poses any danger. The swords are easily dodged, and their drops can be triggered from a safe distance by shooting at them, rendering them little more than another minor inconvenience that Lara gets to solve with hot lead.

Much like the poor leopard she encounters on the way here, on which the camera lingers majestically as she delivers a breathless “magnificent” right before shooting it in the face. I thought this was hilarious and burst out laughing involuntarily, which turned out to be massively out of step with the rest of the room. I even asked the devs about this in the following Q&A: “Is that meant to be funny?”

No, basically. While Lara has no shortage of handy quips, delivered with requisite English public-school plummyness by the wonderful Alix Wilton Regan, this is I’m assured a serious game with a serious tone. So anyone expecting a modicum of self-awareness from this third distinct version of Lara’s original adventure, not counting the recent remaster, will be disappointed.

It highlights a tonal mismatch between the various eras of Lara Croft that this game seeks to blend together. As a nexus point of Crystal Dynamics’ new “unified timeline” for the series, Legacy of Atlantis seeks to replace both the original game and 2007’s Anniversary in the PS1 and Legend timelines, while serving as a sequel to the Survivor Trilogy, which we last visited in 2018’s Shadow of the Tomb Raider . It requires a lot of mental gymnastics to imagine that all of these disparate Laras are the very same bored aristocrat, not least because each of them reflects the time they were conceived in. It’s clear that neither the original games nor the Legend timeline are occurring after the mid-2010s, as clear as it is that this new take on Lara’s original adventure isn’t happening in 1996.

You could argue that it’s all supposed to feel timeless and perpetual, like The Simpsons, but you can’t tell me that pointy PS1 Lara Croft looks like she knows what an iPhone is. There’s also an element of parody to the previous eras, as plenty of Indiana Jones and sixties spy tropes were playfully redeployed as foils for 90s Girl Power, and then again as welcome ballast to the prevailing dourness of post-9/11 Bond movies. A playfulness that the Survivor Trilogy dropped entirely, focusing sharply on the 2010s appropriate misery of being a teenager who unwittingly spends her gap year having to murder dozens of Russian mercenaries while worrying about whether her tetanus shots are up to date.

The point is, all of these flavours of Tomb Raider are distinctly of their time, which is absolutely fine. Smooshing them together into a paste is a weird decision and one that seems to be inspiring some questionable choices, like the inclusion of survival mechanics like crafting and skill trees in this redux of Lara’s original adventure, things that seem to be there just because the last game had them or, worse, because that’s what games are like now. Things that don’t make thematic sense: if this is 2013 Lara finally reaching her prime, her zenith, her most capable self – as the survivor trilogy always promised to be leading to – then why are we still spending the game unlocking her skills?

Why are we “surviving” at all, eating foraged meals cooked in the field, when this isn’t a survival scenario? Lara hasn’t been stranded here, she came to these ruins of her own accord, presumably in a rented jeep. It’s only Greece, you can go on Ryanair for twenty quid. This is a capable explorer who would have a meticulous itinerary and a bag full of protein bars and jerky, she wouldn’t be winging it on the basis of eating boiled moss.

Nor would this classically educated aristocrat seem to need a detective mode scanner thing that gives her puzzle hints and provides handy historical commentary. In fairness, its usage is entirely optional, and seems to be there to address a common criticism of the more recent Tomb Raiders, namely that Lara seems to spend a lot of time chatting to herself.

None of these things are dealbreakers, they’re just prominently questionable choices in a game full of them. As is the decision to employ, then defend, the studio’s use of generative AI in development. Granted, feelings in the community are mixed on this – some care, some don’t, most are probably blissfully unaware of the controversy – but it tends to go down like a shotgunned leopard with enthusiasts, and so using it at all feels like unnecessarily tainting your project before it’s even out.

Because they’ve admitted to using it, it’s hard not to look for evidence of it. I’ll be blunt, the food crafting menus are looking very suspicious. Video game depictions of food are an art form in and of themselves, and often, they are notable for looking absolutely delicious. Who can forget the sweetrolls of Skyrim or the lavish gourmet meals conjured up by Ignis in Final Fantasy 15? In Legacy of Atlantis, though, the food looks kinda disgusting. Despite what the accompanying description says, Lara’s lunches all look rather aptly like slop. Mushy stews of unrecognisable plant matter and meat you’d hesitate to put in a dog.

To be clear, this is all circumstantial – we don’t know for sure if these elements are derived from AI, and the studio for their part has insisted that everything in the final game will be human made or human “refined” – but it demonstrates how damning even a faint association with generative AI can be. Especially if the results are this unappetising.

The game is still many months away from release, and what we’ve seen of it so far is by no means final. There’s time to iron out the kinks and excise the final traces of generative AI that may or may not be plaguing the current build (not that you can un-use genAI any more than a bat can un-shit a temple floor).

As the second remake of a ground-breaking game, Legacy of Atlantis has a lot to live up to. It certainly justifies itself by playing differently from the existing versions: there’s never been a Tomb Raider game quite like this, for better or worse. And though the challenge element has been dramatically reduced in the Damocles Room (and therefore, one presumes, the rest of the adventure), incorporating the giant swords into a traversal puzzle is inspired, and the way it plays out in the demo hints at something fresh: a puzzle with a fixed solution, but multiple routes to reach it.

And it really can’t be stressed enough how beautiful it all is. On a technical level the fidelity in every image is positively retina-searing, but it’s all sumptuously lit and pocked with a gnarly decay that makes the ancient world sing with a sense of history. Lara herself has never looked better, a depiction that successfully blends the slightly cartoony Lara of the Legend trilogy with her naturalistic, mud-caked, cortisol-saturated counterpart of Tomb Raider 2013. New Lara spent her youth avoiding certain death in some of the most deadly corners of the earth, from Syria to Siberia, yet moves with all the balletic flourishes that the Survivor Trilogy sidelined in favour of Uncharted-style handhold grappling. Every jump, flip, and bullet-time whip exudes joy: this is a Lara who revels in being Lara. She even does that handstand backflip thing when hoisting herself onto a platform (in the build we saw, a little too often, but I heavily suspect it was dialled up for this demo).

There’s a lot to love here. A celebration of all Tomb Raiders past and present, one that treats all of the previous eras as equally important to the series’ legacy, is refreshingly inclusive. In these sorts of franchise overhauls, someone’s favourite usually gets overlooked in pursuit of whatever is deemed to be the most iconic or fundamental. To have a project here that treats the whole thing as gospel is admirable, if dauntingly hard to chew.

As someone who grew up with Lara and has enjoyed every iteration of Tomb Raider, I desperately want to be on board for this new, unified journey. But a mixture of dubious choices, mechanical and ethical, are making it a tough sell at the moment. I very much doubt Lara would choose to consume suspicious looking slop if any alternatives were available, and neither should anyone else.

Jim Trinca is a Video Producer at IGN, and when he isn't fawning over Assassin's Creed, he can be found watching Star Trek and eating stuff. Follow him on @jimtrinca.bsky.social , and check out The Trinca Perspective playlist over on IGN's YouTube channel!

As someone who grew up with Lara and has enjoyed every iteration of Tomb Raider, I desperately want to be on board for this new, unified journey. But a mixture of dubious choices, mechanical and ethical, are making it a tough sell at the moment. I very much doubt Lara would choose to consume suspicious looking slop if any alternatives were available, and neither should anyone else.

articles.title: Scientists Put Caterpillars in an Ultraquiet Chamber to Learn How They Hear Without Ears
articles.description: The research could do more than help unlock the mystery of caterpillar hearing. It could also help make microphones better.

h2: What Happens in the Anechoic Chamber

contentBlocks.text: In a quiet summer garden, a caterpillar perches on a branch, munching serenely on leaves. A moment later it freezes. It senses danger—and just in time. From behind, a wasp approaches, sizing up its prey.
Tobacco hornworm caterpillars don’t look like they have ears, and yet they’re able to sense predators such as wasps. How does the caterpillar know a wasp is approaching?

Scientists do not fully understand how this caterpillar’s senses work, but we are part of a team of biologists and engineers who want to figure it out. Our ongoing research suggests that tobacco hornworms can hear using tiny, supersensitive hairs on their body.

Understanding the intricate biological mechanisms that allow this organism to perceive and interact with its environment would help solve a mystery of the natural world. It could also help scientists design new, cheaper microphone technology.
Because the hornworms’ hairs are so sensitive, we have to study them in complete silence. And where better to study hearing than in the complete silence of an anechoic chamber ?
What Happens in the Anechoic Chamber

What happens outside the anechoic chamber stays outside the anechoic chamber, because it is meticulously built that way. Anechoic chambers are some of the quietest places in the world. They are engineered specifically to block the entry of any undesired sounds. Heavy-duty steel springs support the “floating” chamber and keep it from touching the ground. This detachment isolates the space from outside vibrations or noise.

In such a chamber, we studied the caterpillars’ responses to vibrations. Every day for a year, we set up a caterpillar on a platform and sent vibrations toward the platform at a variety of intensities.

To measure the movement and precise vibrations that traveled through the platform the caterpillar sat on, we used a device called an accelerometer . In response to vibrations, we sometimes saw the caterpillars jump; at other times they twitched or even shuddered from the sheer physical force.

Through our observations, we pinned down the specific threshold where the caterpillars stopped reacting to vibrations. Any vibration weaker than that magnitude, and the caterpillar wouldn’t visibly react at all.

After noticing this consistent pattern, we decided to test more caterpillars inside the anechoic chamber, but this time using airborne sound as the stimulus. The idea here was that if the caterpillars are more sensitive to sound than they are to vibrations, they are probably hearing airborne sounds independent of any vibrations.

Sound is broadly defined as a form of vibration or energy that becomes audible, meaning you can hear it with your ears. But here’s the catch: Sound also causes objects to vibrate. To make sure the caterpillar wasn’t just sensing the sound’s vibrations through the platform, we also used the accelerometer to measure the vibrations that the platform experienced from the sound. Our goal was to compare the platform vibrations produced in two distinct scenarios: when sound through the air was used as the stimulus versus when just direct vibrations were used as the stimulus.

We noticed that this time the caterpillars continued reacting to the sound even beneath their threshold of response to the direct vibrations. This finding suggested that they were hearing the airborne sounds.
Finding the Caterpillars’ “Ears”
So, where are their “ears?” Or rather, what are their “ears?”
There are two ways of hearing sound: from the sound waves’ pressure and from the velocity of the particles making up the sound waves.

For the longest time, scientists have associated hearing with tympanal organs . A tympanal organ in most mammals is a membrane that vibrates in response to pressure from sound waves. Its vibration moves the bone structures adjacent to it as well.
In most insects that respond to sound pressure, the structure analogous to the tympanal organ is a sac filled with air. They perceive any vibrations to this sac as sound.

But caterpillars pose a challenge to this typical hearing system, because they can hear but do not have obvious tympanal membranes. After digging into some past research and examining the caterpillars under the microscope, we spotted the distinctive hairs on their bodies.

Thus, our next project began. We removed their hairs and compared their responses to sound before and after the hair removal. Sometimes we surgically removed all the hairs by plucking them with tweezers under the microscope, and sometimes we strategically targeted a few.

The result was striking: The caterpillars’ defensive reactions decreased dramatically across various sound frequencies depending on which specific hairs were removed. While our research continues, and we haven’t yet published our results in a journal, this work is allowing us to piece together the caterpillar hearing puzzle and investigate which of these hairs are tuned to register different sound frequencies.

This line of research into how insects hear sounds using specialized, microscopic hairs could inspire a new generation of acoustic tools. Standard microphones are devices that contain membranes within them that can detect sound pressure levels . By mimicking these biological systems, such as using structures like these hairs in place of membranes, future microphones could be designed to instead measure the air particle velocity caused by sound, alongside the sound pressure levels.

Microphones that can detect air particle velocity would also be able to determine the direction of origin of the sound wave. In the case of microphone designs for hearing aids , a microphone that is able to track both sound pressure and air particle velocity could provide the user with information on both volume and direction of the sound wave. And studying caterpillars’ hearing systems and imitating how their “hearing hairs” work could inspire such directional microphones.

articles.title: The Watch World Went Crazy This Week. Here Are the 10 You Need to See
articles.description: The main action took place at Geneva Watch Days, but others dialed in remotely to make sure it wasn't just a Swiss party.

contentBlocks.text: While Watches and Wonders every April is undoubtedly the watch world's main event of the year , Geneva Watch Days—which inauspiciously launched in 2020, the year Covid was declared a pandemic —is now establishing itself as a serious follow-up. Big brands can hold back key releases and gain valuable space to shout about new pieces away from the horological hubbub of W&W.

A second bite of the marketing apple in the latter half of the year seems like a good idea, as Swiss watch exports declined again in 2025 after a drop in 2024. However, despite America's tariff seesaw , the US is still by far the single largest market for Swiss watches. And, more positively for watch fans , signs suggest the industry downturn could be over .
Here are WIRED's picks of the best watches that dropped this week.

Inspired by the 1960s Breitling Navitimer 806 Mk5 worn by none other than Miles Davis, this manual-wind B09 with a display caseback takes cues from the original beyond the manual winding: the Twin Jet logo, reverse-panda dial, faux-aged cream-colored lume, and the original 41-mm dimensions. The pitch is that you get what made the 806 Mk5 great but with a modern overhaul. This model is limited to 500 pieces: You could go for the stainless steel on calf leather strap for $8,900, but we think you'd be kind of blue (sorry) to miss the superb bracelet model, complete with round vents, for $9,600 .

Not part of Geneva Watch Days, here's something genuinely new from Casio's G-Shock line that's leaked and could break the internet . The GAC-2500 series is a resin analog lineup supposedly built from the DNA of the DW-5000C , the very first G-Shock made back in 1983. But that's not the real story of this piece. Much like the famous “ CasiOak ” that many G-Shock fans love for its passing resemblance to Audemars Piguet's Royal Oak , this GAC-2500 series has more than a whiff of Patek Philippe’s Nautilus about it.

So far, nicknames like “CasioNaut” and “CasioTilus” are being thrown around. Leaks suggest four resin colors at launch in November—white, black, green, and yellow—and the price is rumored to be 20,900 Japanese yen (about $134) each. There might be stainless-steel versions too—the GMC-2500D series, going for about $320.

Following Miss Piggy and Kermit editions, Oris clearly feels it's on to a winning formula with Muppets collaborations. This one is more interesting than the solid pink-and-green colors of the previous dalliances. The Gonzo is a reworking of Oris' ProPilot X but with subtle, classy nods to Gonzo the Great that chime perfectly with the subtle, classy performance art that is his trademark. While the showman himself appears on the watch’s mainspring, at 11 o’clock, the thumping 10-day power reserve indicator is a red chili, inspired by one of Gonzo’s favorite shirts. Such subtlety comes at a cost, however, as at $10,500 , the Gonzo is twice the price of a Kermit.

A volume play from Zenith, and a good one. Bringing its famed El Primero movement to a cheaper—sorry, “more accessible”—price, the Solo Sport is a 40-mm steel diver watch, not a chronograph, with 200 meters of water resistance and a unidirectional rotating ceramic bezel. The black ceramic dial reveals the movement's capabilities, with a high-frequency pattern and “Shark tooth” minute track, showcasing the caliber’s prize feature: 5 Hz or 36,000 vph (vibrations per hour). You can grab this for $10,900 with a date window, but those in the know will get the cleaner no-date for $9,800 .

Not physically at Geneva Watch Days either, Swatch Group's Hamilton decided to crash the party and release an upgraded version of its successful Interstellar Murph timepiece. Dialing up the model's association with Christopher Nolan's classic sci-fi film , Hamilton has added a version to its collection with a dappled “comet-inspired” face where the blue center is intended to reflect the glow of ionized gases in space. Whether you understand this cosmic connection is immaterial when the outcome is this pleasing. Sensibly, Hamilton has chosen to release the new Murph in the preferred 38-mm sizing at $995 .

More comets? Yes indeed. Founded in 2017 by designer and photographer Ming Thein, this independent watch brand is known for a winning blend of refined aesthetics and innovative engineering. Here, this 40-mm stainless-steel worldtimer features a first-of-its-kind, patent-pending system for adjusting the time to account for daylight saving. Borrowing its name from the de Havilland Comet , the world’s first commercial jet airliner, the watch's split bezel divides cities according to whether they observe daylight saving. Those that don’t are fixed on the inner bezel, but the ones that do are on the outer ring. Rotating this outer bezel advances only the affected cities by one hour. Clever.

The limited run of 200 pieces has already been snapped up, but you can register online for future availability. If you get lucky, shun the $9,750 leather strap model for the $10,875 Polymesh bracelet version.

Another no-show at Geneva Watch Days was this new piece from Tudor. Well, not new exactly. After discontinuing the North Flag as recently as 2021, Tudor is bringing it back. Originally launched in 2015 at Baselworld, the North Flag was the first Tudor to boast one of the company's in-house movements. The new 40-mm “reissue” (now Northflag, not North Flag) sports a 24-hour hand for a second time zone. Water resistance is a respectable 100 meters, and there's a display caseback, too. Inside is Tudor's 4-Hz METAS-certified automatic movement. The uncluttered, functional black dial with yellow seconds and 24-hour hands is nicely contrasted by blue lume for the hands and markers. This watch, plus an integrated bracelet with Tudor's T-Fit micro-adjustment in the clasp, goes for $5,525 .

Bulgari's multi-award-winning watch line now stars the “Dazzle,” an 80-piece limited-edition, super-thin Octo Finissimo built around the brand's 40-mm sandblasted titanium case. Despite its slender proportions, the watch manages a 60-hour power reserve. However, the highlight is the laser-engraved pattern on the case and bracelet, which looks more like it belongs in the world of Minecraft than horology. The geometric pattern is actually based upon “dazzle camouflage” devised by British zoologist John Graham Kerr, who proposed (to Winston Churchill, no less, in 1914) that the disruptive design would, much like zebra stripes, break up the perceived outline of ships at sea. Bulgari's Octo “Dazzle” will set you back $18,300.

The resurrection of Gallet, 200 years after its foundation in La Chaux-de-Fonds, completes Breitling's “House of Brands,” with Breitling taking on the center ground of the Swiss luxury watch market, Universal Genève going high-end, and now the relaunched Gallet slipping in below them both. The first model from the much-anticipated Gallet revival is the Flying Officer, and it's landing in two variations: the Flying Officer Chronograph 40 and the Flying Officer Automatic 40. The 40-mm chrono in light blue at $4,400 would be our pick, along with the orange Automatic 40 at $2,900 .

Never a brand to shy away from doing something more than a little “out there,” Hublot has given its iconic Big Bang Original a new feel with a fabric makeover thanks to a velvet-like rubber invention. Two Soft Touch models see the case, bezel, dial, and strap wrapped in a specially developed textured rubber compound. Created through an overmolding process, the unique microscopic surface structure is composed of thousands of fine micro-elements, creating softness to the touch while supposedly keeping the durability and resistance of Hublot's signature rubber. The 43-mm model comes in black, but the red at $29,000 is tantalizing.

articles.title: 14 Predictions for the September 2026 Nintendo Direct and Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct
articles.description: IGN's Logan Plant shares 14 predictions for the pair of Nintendo Directs airing in the coming days.

h1: 14 Predictions for the September 2026 Nintendo Direct and Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct
h2: IGN's Logan Plant shares 14 predictions for the pair of Nintendo Directs airing in the coming days.

contentBlocks.text: Nintendo is hosting two Directs in the coming days , and it’s pretty much all I’ve been thinking about since the announcement. On Tuesday, September 8, it’s The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct, followed by a more general Nintendo Direct on Wednesday, September 9. While we wait, it's predictions time!

Before we start, a couple of disclaimers: these are all purely my guesses based on public information and my analysis of Nintendo’s release patterns, and nothing more. Nothing here is based on any inside information. But, I will be discussing a couple of relevant leaks over the last few months, so if you have been steering clear of information like that, you may not want to read on.
Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct Predictions

Zelda is my favorite series, so I’m buzzing thinking about all the possibilities we could see Tuesday morning. But I’m trying to keep things realistic in this piece and only sharing predictions that I think have a legitimate chance of happening.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s Full Reveal

This will undoubtedly be the centerpiece of the presentation. We’ve only seen a few seconds of footage of the Ocarina of Time remake , which is set to come out in 2026. So, now’s the time for the full reveal trailer and release date. I can’t wait for this one; my imagination has been running wild over this remake for the last three months, and we’re finally going to see more about the scope of this remake. Is it faithful, or more of a reimagining? What does the kingdom of Hyrule look like beyond Link’s treehouse? All that and more will likely be answered by a more conventional trailer that gives us a proper look at the remake.

I don’t know exactly what Ocarina of Time will look like, but the teaser trailer from earlier this year tells me Nintendo is very confident in this game. You don’t set the internet’s imagination on fire with a 10-second tease of Link’s treehouse if you don’t have really satisfying answers to share when you do finally pull the curtain back, and I expect the Ocarina of Time remake to be a pretty big deal.
Ocarina of Time's Release Date

As for a release date, I’m expecting Ocarina of Time to arrive on Thursday, November 12. Nintendo doesn’t have a game dated for November yet (Fire Emblem arrives this month, with Nintendo Switch Sports slated for October), and it never misses putting out a big game in the weeks before Black Friday. Knowing it’s coming this year, Zelda feels primed for that spot. Nintendo is extremely unlikely to release a game on Thanksgiving (that’s Thursday, November 26 in the U.S.), and it has no reason to go head-to-head with Grand Theft Auto VI on November 19. That just leaves November 5 and 12 as available Thursdays to launch a game. A few weeks back, the Nintendo UK store briefly dated a couple of Kirby Air Riders amiibo for November 12 , and Nintendo typically launches amiibo the same day as a first-party game, even if the franchises aren’t related. That date has since been removed, but I’m still pretty locked in on November 12 as Ocarina of Time’s release date.
Ocarina of Time amiibo

With amiibo on the mind, I’m hopeful we’ll get a glimpse of a new amiibo line for Ocarina of Time alongside the reveal. Zelda games typically get tie-in amiibo figures (Echoes of Wisdom is a rare recent exception), so I’m expecting we’ll see figures of Young Link and Adult Link at the very least.
Special Edition Nintendo Switch 2 and Pro Controller

A few weeks ago, allegedly leaked designs surfaced for a Zelda-themed Nintendo Switch 2 console and Pro Controller. These don’t appear to be branded for Ocarina of Time specifically, but rather for the 40th anniversary as a whole. If they’re legitimate, it'd make the most sense to see the products formally announced on Tuesday, potentially alongside my predicted November 12 release for Ocarina of Time. articles.title: 'No One Puts Double Fine Out of Business Except for Me' — Tim Schafer Explains How He Kept Double Fine Afloat After Leaving Xbox
articles.description: Tim Schafer, game designer and founder of Psychonauts developer Double Fine, gave a strong response after Xbox divested the studio as part of its massive restructuring efforts this summer.

h1: 'No One Puts Double Fine Out of Business Except for Me' — Tim Schafer Explains How He Kept Double Fine Afloat After Leaving Xbox

contentBlocks.text: Tim Schafer, game designer and founder of Psychonauts developer Double Fine, gave a strong response after Xbox divested the studio as part of its massive restructuring efforts this summer.

Speaking with Bloomberg's Jason Schreier in a September 2026 interview , Schafer admitted that he knew something was up before Xbox’s divestment was officially announced — but he wasn’t about to go down without a fight.

"You’re like, 'Wait a second, we’re not going out like this,'" Schafer explained. "Some people said, 'I’m checking out, this is one too many battles for me.’ But for the rest of us, it’s like a creative awakening."

"No one puts Double Fine out of business except for me," he continued. "Asha’s not going to shoot my dog. I’m going to shoot it. But I’m not going to shoot it, because it’s going to do great. A lot of people want to walk the dog."

Thankfully, Double Fine was able to retain its intellectual property and become fully independent, though it did have to lay off a quarter of its staff as a result of this change. That isn’t stopping it from making more games, though, as the developer recently published a Kickstarter for its next project — with the addendum that if it raises $100 million, they’ll also make Brutal Legend 2.

"We’ve been through a lot this year," Schafer told Schreier. "A lot of it is very soul-sucking stuff. Inner conflict, threats of extermination, long negotiations, strenuous hard tradeoffs with lawyers. Tons of demoralizing stuff."
And yet, in spite of these challenges, Schafer says he’s been able to find a creative spark that has invigorated both himself and the remaining team at Double Fine.

"This is the good fight. Can we think of a great idea for a game that we can actually do for the right budget, that can get to this publisher who’s interested in these types of games? This kind of problem-solving is soul-enriching. Using creativity to solve problems is what gets us up in the morning. So it is hard, and it is scary and it is stressful, but it’s at least putting some fire back into the bellies of the team and me," he said.

Xbox has undergone a slew of major changes as CEO Asha Sharma works to make the company profitable again. Shedding Double Fine was part of that change, as well as massive layoffs that affected roughly 3,200 employees.

Sharma has been fairly transparent with Xbox’s financial state and future plans, most recently telling the BBC that the brand’s next generation console, Project Helix, will include a “family of devices,” though she notably declined to comment if it’ll have a disc drive or not.
In other Double Fine news, the developer shadow dropped Keeper , a formerly Xbox-exclusive title, on PlayStation 5 today now that it's no longer tied to the company.

h1: gamescom Apologizes for Its Initial Response to Thefts, Promises Improved Security Measures
h2: "We understand what this has cost you, and we should have said so from the very first moment."

contentBlocks.text: gamescom has provided a second response regarding the theft of developers’ equipment during its event, offering an apology for its initial reaction to the ordeal.

On August 28, 2026, indie developer Ryan Laley uploaded a video to X/Twitter claiming that all of his laptops had been stolen at gamescom. He wasn’t the only one affected; several other developers spoke out with similar stories, saying their equipment had also been pilfered at the event.
gamescom responded to the ordeal on August 29, writing that while it was "very sad" about the situation, it "would like to inform [attendees] about general security regulations."

articles.title: Halloween: The Game Review So Far
articles.description: So far this asymmetrical horror game is more trick than treat.

h1: Halloween: The Game Review So Far
h2: So far this asymmetrical horror game is more trick than treat.

contentBlocks.text: Plenty of things are terrifying about a man in a boiler suit creeping up behind you, but it's hard to be scared of Halloween: The Game's Michael Myers when he strolls around the neighborhood with all the urgency of a retiree on a golf course. Admittedly, my early experience with the latest asymmetrical survival horror based on a famous movie came without the obligatory day one patch, so everything I’ve seen so far comes with that giant, flashing caveat. But after several hours, my immediate reaction is that this just isn't ready. I would barely think it’s ready if it were labeled asan early access game, which it’s not. Clumsy, buggy, and often frustrating, Halloween: The Game seems in need of considerable polish and bug squishing.

Developer Illfonic is, of course, almost synonymous with asymmetrical horror at this point, if not quite able to break the stranglehold Behaviour Interactive has with Dead by Daylight. In keeping with the traditions of the genre, you either play on your own as the killer, Michael Myers, and rampage through the town, or you work with up to three other humans and a handful of AI companions to loot items and keep yourself alive long enough to find, open, and escape the streets of Haddonfield on Halloween night in 1978.
Halloween: The Game Gameplay Screenshots

Because of Illfonic's back catalog, I came in with high expectations, and knowing Halloween creator John Carpenter was also involved sent them soaring even further. You'd think, with the best part of a decade's learning and all that asym trial and error behind it, Halloween: The Game would be the most polished of all Illfonic's games. But — so far at least — that just doesn't seem to be the case.

Animations are broken or missing completely. I've had hard crashes that sent me back to my PS5 dash, averaging at least one an hour. Combat is beyond janky — several times now, I've stabbed a player and had my weapon phase right through them. Often the sound gets messed up, so when I open a door to my left , I hear it to my right , which is hugely irritating given sound is vital to a stealth horror game. And on two occasions, a quick time event bugged out and trapped me in a broken animation, giving Myers all the time in the world to step up right behind me. That was just as much fun and not-at-all-frustrating as it sounds.

The NPC AI is also hysterically stupid. Once, playing as Myers, I (loudly) busted through a front door and found all three remaining NPCs in the same room, still standing at the same window. I had executed two before the remaining one decided it was time to make a run for it.

It's galling because there are some excellent ideas here. I had a great time with The Texas Chain Saw Massacre 's spin on asymmetrical horror back in 2023, but within days it was clear no one wanted to play as Leatherface because it was so much easier — and considerably more fun — to clock up XP and escape as a survivor.

In Halloween: The Game, however, Illfonic seems to have really worked to balance the odds between killer and civilian, and Myers is a blast to play. Even though he never, ever runs, making it next to impossible to take out a player if they've seen you, his special abilities — snuffing out all the lights in the immediate area; jumping from shadow to shadow; detecting nearby players — help mitigate that deeply unsatisfactory walking speed, especially if you nail the timing. Plus, the execution mechanic is a neat shortcut if you manage to get close enough to… well, execute it. The death animations, if often out of sync, are brilliantly brutal, too, particularly if you manage to catch a civilian, by a window or next to an electric oven. (I'm sure there's more still to discover!)

Best of all, this isn't just four humans against one killer. As Myers, your job is to wipe the map clean of all survivors, human and NPC alike. As a civilian, you need to creep around the deliciously 70s-inspired maps — everything, from the cars to the decor to the rotary phones, is on point here, not to mention the fashion! — quietly warning NPCs and instructing them to either hide, follow you, or escape.

There are plenty of items to gather as you creep through residential homes, including offensive weapons, defensive tools, and a host of goodies to bolster the odds of getting out of there unscathed. You'll never be able to take Myers out completely — just like the movies, this is a dude who does not know how to take the hint and die — but you can temporarily immobilize him with the right timing and the right equipment.

That said, why do we have to sit and watch Myers finish killing off idiot NPCs if all the human players are already dead? You're given QTEs when spectating — I hate them; there are too many, they're too boring, and I swear there's occasionally an input delay — but it's so tedious, especially as the maps are pretty chunky and make hunting down one last survivor time-consuming.
Vikki Blake's Most Terrifying Horror Games Ever List

And it just doesn't perform well. Even beyond the poor AI and broken QTEs, I experienced numerous crashes, rubberbanding, and framerate drops for no discernible reason. Characters sometimes walked three feet off the ground. Interacting with items is completely hit-or-miss — half the time you can pick stuff up or remove a chain with a bolt cutter; half the time you cannot. Oh, and sometimes you can open a door, step through it, lock it, and then find yourself back outside the front, unable to get back in.

Like I said, I need to play on the launch patch before finalizing my thoughts — but, generally speaking, a day one update is rarely a miracle fix for all of a review build’s issues. Still, I'll be back once I've spent some time on the live servers with both the single and multiplayer modes (so far the former has completely underwhelmed me — again, mostly due to idiotic NPCs). I'd also like to better understand how the card perk system works and experiment with all the civilians' passive abilities. For now, though, it's difficult to recommend Halloween: The Game to anyone other than a horror fan with a Michael Myers shrine in their home (now that's a scary thought) or those with deep, deep affection for asymmetrical games.

selected.title: Insomniac Clears the Air After Marvel's Wolverine Fans Confuse Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke
selected.description: Insomniac Games has cleared the air after a new trailer for Marvel's Wolverine had fans confusing Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke.

h1: Insomniac Clears the Air After Marvel's Wolverine Fans Confuse Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke

contentBlocks.text: Insomniac Games has cleared the air after a new trailer for Marvel's Wolverine had fans confusing Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke.

If you thought the launch trailer for the PlayStation 5-exclusive video game would come and go without controversy, I've got bad news. Despite coming in at a little less than a minute and a half long, Marvel's Wolverine managed to kick up a storm of confusion online after fans spotted what they believed was a new character wielding a familiar-looking purple energy sword.

In comments across YouTube, Instagram, X/Twitter, and other social media platforms, you don't have to look too hard to find watchers questioning if the sneering villain featured in the launch trailer was Psylocke. Psylocke is an energy-wielding mutant who's been known to show up across various X-Men stories in the past, so when a glowing sword showed up in Marvel's Wolverine, many believed it to be a grand character reveal.
Well, it's not, and Insomniac has done its best to make that clear.
Deathstrike. #WolverinePS5 pic.twitter.com/koWhS5v3HG

The post above was published earlier today and labels the sword user as Lady Deathstrike. The PlayStation developer didn't outright say it's trying to quiet the noise that's emerged in the days following the trailer's reveal, but judging by the comments, many are shocked any clarification was needed in the first place.
"The fact it has to be stated is so crazy to me," one user said . "Larp monsters are everywhere."
"No that’s Psylocke, some guy told me and he’s for sure right," another user joked .

It really does seem to be the purple sword that's to blame here because, as some have noted, Lady Deathstrike looks nothing like Psylocke. The version of the character featured in Marvel's Wolverine doesn't exactly have a comic-accurate design, but her vest and hair do more to link her to Lady Deathstrike than the character many were making her out to be.

There's also the fact that Insomniac has talked about Lady Deathstrike being in Marvel's Wolverine before, with the launch trailer also being far from the first time we've even seen her in the game. For example, one early look at her new design arrived in July's Ain't No Hero trailer , while a GIF the studio posted on social media showed her looking down on viewers.

These aren't clips of her doing anything you'd expect Psylocke to do either. This version has been shown attacking Logan with Lady Deathstrike's instantly recognizable finger claws on full display multiple times. Why she's using that sword or where it came from remains a mystery, but whatever the reason, it's not because she's actually Psylocke. That's not to say that character isn't in the game at all; other X-Men regulars like Jean Grey and Sabretooth are confirmed to make an apperance. If Psylockie is in the game, though, Insomniac hasn't publicly said a thing about her.

Logan will at least take on Lady Deathstrike – not Psylocke – when Marvel's Wolverine launches for PS5 September 15, 2026. Meanwhile, the launch trailer actually arrived as part of a recent State of Play presentation from Sony, which you can catch up on here . For more, you can check out IGN's last full preview and our breakdown for the game's many, many suits .

h1: The Blood of Dawnwalker Passes 1 Million Copies Sold in Just 2 Days

contentBlocks.text: Single-player RPG and new IP The Blood of Dawnwalker has sold 1 million copies just two days after its launch, publisher Bandai Namco and developer Rebel Wolves have announced.

Official social media accounts for the first-time developer's new game confirmed the news with a celebratory graphic today. The milestone was reached just 48 hours after The Blood of Dawnwalker launched for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S September 3.
"Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community!" Rebel Wolves said in a message to fans.
Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community! ❤ pic.twitter.com/9fNqO8gNGB

An official summary for The Blood of Dawnwalker describes it as an "open-world dark fantasy action RPG set in 14th-century Europe." In this first chapter, players take the role of Coen, a "human by day and vampire by night" who is fighting for his family in a narrative shaped by player choice. It also happens to have an in-game clock that sees Coen's story take place through a 30-day period . It's something some players love – and others don't .

Reaching 1 million copies sold in such a short amount of time would be an impressive feat for any game, but there are a few reasons it's especially noteworthy for the Rebel Wolves team. This is the studio's first major release since it was founded in 2022 . Led by The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt director and Cyberpunk 2077 co-director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz, The Blood of Dawnwalker is also a new IP. The Warsaw-based studio previously released a CGI teaser to tease how sequels could potentially expand on its dark fantasy formula in new and interesting ways.

"The CGI teaser shows where the dark fantasy saga is heading," Bandai Namco said in a June press release. "Players can see Coen in completely different surroundings than the ones they are used to – a modern, 21st-century setting, offering a glimpse of where the overarching plot ultimately leads. As the developers revealed, the next installments of the Dawnwalker franchise will span centuries, continents, and cultures across the globe."

selected.title: There May Not Be an iPhone 18 This Year
selected.description: Apple is expected to announce several products at its September event next week—including a folding phone—but the iPhone 18 might not be among them. It would be a first for the company.

contentBlocks.text: Every year around this time, Apple announces new iPhones . The products go on sale soon after, usually ranging from a base model to more premium and more expensive Pro models. But this year will likely be different—not just because the company has a brand-new CEO .

Apple’s iPhone event will be held on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern), announced last week with the title “Surprise and Shine!” If you tune into the livestream, expect the announcement of an iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and, if all the rumors and widely held analyst expectations are true, the first look at an Apple foldable device .

Based on leaks and the ongoing tech rumor mill and its decent track record for figuring these things out, Apple is expected to prioritize its more expensive, premium devices this year and hold off on announcing its base model iPhone 18. That cheaper model is rumored to launch in the spring of 2027, potentially alongside an iPhone 18e and maybe a second-generation iPhone Air .

Why the drastic change in strategy? It may be due to the ongoing memory shortage , which has made just about everything more expensive . Apple hasn’t been spared. In June, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that Apple would raise product prices to keep up with manufacturing costs.

“Our assumption is that they're going to be launching three models in the fall, the premium side of the models of the 18 series,” says Nabila Popal , a senior director of data and analytics at IDC. “Then the mid/budget devices will be launched in the spring.”

Popal says it's a smart strategic move because Apple is aiming to spread out its revenue between a usually very strong fourth quarter and a typically much weaker spring quarter the following year. Apple’s portfolio has also expanded, and the iPhone Pro and Pro Max lineup are more enticing for people already prepared to spend the money on a new iPhone .

When components become more expensive, companies have three real options: Eat the costs, raise prices, or, as Apple seems to be doing, lean into it. By moving its cheaper options to a later date, Apple can drum up excitement for its bigger, better, pricier offerings. When it charges more for those, it is likely to be less off-putting than making a cheap phone even more expensive. It’s part of a “premiumization” of devices, as Popal calls it, that Apple hopes to leverage and build hype for its pricier options.
Shawn DuBravac , chief economist at the Global Electronics Association, tells WIRED he is optimistic about what these kinds of rising prices ultimately mean for customers.

“Throughout the history of time, the deflationary pressures of technology have always flowed to the consumer,” DuBravac says. “I'm confident that will be the case again. It just will take some time for the markets to solidify.” In other words, new technologies launch with a high price, but manufacturing efficiencies and competition inevitably drive costs down for consumers.

That may not be the case anytime soon for folding phones , which are seeing higher prices than ever. Samsung’s entire 2026 Galaxy Z folding smartphone range saw price increases, as did Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro Fold , and Motorola’s Razr 2026 models . Apple’s folding iPhone is rumored to cost around $2,000.

To help mitigate those high costs, Apple is turning to financing options and trade-in programs. In July, the company launched an iPhone leasing program that lets people pay a monthly fee to rent the newest iPhones, then swap them out when a new device releases. The program will undoubtedly help more people afford the newest devices, but ownership advocates have criticized it, saying it keeps you from truly owning and managing your device. It also fits Apple’s broader effort to turn all of its products into a subscription service .
“The way most consumers buy Apple phones is through financing or trade-in programs,” Popal says. “We can expect a lot more aggressive trade-ins to help cushion that.”

Thanks to the memory crisis and price increases, all smartphones are getting more costly to make. Less expensive phones become less appealing for manufacturers to prioritize, and leading smartphone brands have started to see them as far less economical to produce.

On the flip side, demand for refurbished devices has been climbing for a while now, with sales of used devices growing even as new phone sales slow down. More people are looking to save money or purchase more eco-friendly products.
“The days of the cheap smartphone are over,” Popal says.

selected.title: OpenAI Agents Hacked Another Website
selected.description: Plus: Tens of millions of US and Canadian drivers’ licenses go up for sale on the dark web, the US military finally tries to tackle the risk online ad data poses to troops, and more.

h2: Before Hugging Face, OpenAI Agents Took Over a German Website to Create a Message Board
More Than 153 Million US and Canadian Driver’s Licenses for Sale Online
US Military Disables Ad Trackers After Years of Warnings
Spyware Notifications Make Up “Largest Documented Wave” of Surveillance in Serbia

contentBlocks.text: After reporting last week that the surveillance company Flock Safety is building an AI search tool for law enforcement, WIRED reconstructed Flock’s latest search tool from code that the company sends to a police officer’s browser and uncovered key details about how the tool works.

OpenAI said this week that its Astra model, which will have a private release soon, is its first model with cybersecurity-related capabilities that the company defines as posing a “critical” risk in public release. Meanwhile, the AI chatbot platforms Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok all suffered outages on Thursday at nearly the exact same time. But while xAI said the Grok outage resulted from issues at a Memphis data center, the causes of OpenAI's and Anthropic’s outages are unclear.

The US has been using a high-energy laser to shoot down drones near the Mexico border as part of an initiative to adopt new-generation directed-energy weapons capable of detecting, tracking, and destroying drones with a concentrated beam of light. And as part of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement inquiry into the identities of protesters who entered a Minnesota church in March, Homeland Security Investigations agents have subpoenaed the outdoor retailer REI for information about every customer who bought a specific green beanie over the past two years.
Plus, research that revealed nine vulnerabilities with impacts on ATM encryption points to broader weaknesses in the software supply chain.
And there’s more. Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Click the headlines to read the full stories. And stay safe out there.
Before Hugging Face, OpenAI Agents Took Over a German Website to Create a Message Board

OpenAI agents on an unauthorized tear hijacked a German website beginning in May to use it as a message board for communicating and collaborating with other agents, according to new research . The incident is reminiscent of the now infamous Hugging Face debacle in which OpenAI agents in a test environment went rogue and developed a vibrant message board for collaborating on attempting to escape their containment, before ultimately breaching the open source AI platform Hugging Face in July. The revelation of the May episode is particularly significant because OpenAI reportedly learned about it weeks ago but did not disclose it. Meanwhile, last week, the company finally released a long-promised postmortem of the Hugging Face incident that raised as many questions as it answered .
More Than 153 Million US and Canadian Driver’s Licenses for Sale Online

This week, a new dark-web service called Nexus started selling around 153 million driver's licenses from the US and Canada, along with 10 million ID cards and millions more travel documents and international IDs, according to Brian Krebs , a longtime independent security reporter. Krebs was first alerted to the service after cybercriminals posted an example of the files and included his license. The tens of millions of records—which reportedly increased by 400,000 over 24 hours—appear to have come from an ID verification service, with the criminals behind the trove saying they have access to a “major” verification company. While it’s unclear which company exactly that may be, according to Kreb’s report, the Nexus service was taken offline shortly after he reported that FBI officials were investigating.
US Military Disables Ad Trackers After Years of Warnings

The US military has begun disabling the advertising identifiers that apps and advertising companies use to track phones and computers in an attempt to make it harder for foreign adversaries to use commercially available location data to track American forces overseas, Reuters reported Friday.

The changes follow years of disclosures that US forces deployed abroad have been targeted using commercially available location data. In 2024, a joint WIRED investigation with Germany’s Bayerischer Rundfunk and Netzpolitik.org obtained an advertising dataset that identified thousands of devices appearing at US military and intelligence sites, including an air base where US nuclear weapons are believed to be stored. At the time, Defense Department spokesperson Javan Rasnake told WIRED that the Pentagon was aware geolocation services could put personnel at risk and said service members in Europe were reminded to follow operational-security practices.

Now, the Air Force, Army, Navy, and US Special Operations Command say they have disabled advertising IDs on at least some military devices, with several of the changes taking effect only this year. It is still unclear exactly how these protections are being enforced. US senator Ron Wyden and Representative Pat Harrigan are now asking the Pentagon to investigate whether its safeguards are adequate.

Mike Yeagley, the technologist who warned Pentagon officials as far back as 2016 that commercially available phone data could expose US troops—at one point demonstrating the risk by tracing devices to a covert US outpost in Syria—says the military’s new fix may already be outdated. “The app is the risk, and there are two and a half million of them in the App Store alone,” Yeagley tells WIRED. “The remedy is architectural: Constrain what an app can extract from the device in the first place.”
Spyware Notifications Make Up “Largest Documented Wave” of Surveillance in Serbia

In August, Apple sent out its latest batch of spyware notifications to people in 110 countries. The alerts, which arrive on people’s phones and in emails, say their owners' iPhones have been targeted by “mercenary” spyware but don’t go as far as naming the software creators. This latest batch of notifications, according to a report by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, says 14 members of Serbia’s civil society were targeted with spyware , with at least one of them being infected by the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware. Among those targeted, according to Serbian rights group the Share Foundation, were members of the country’s student movement, two politicians, and activists. The group called it the “largest documented wave of such surveillance in the country to date.”
